speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions or comments, the Hon. Member for Algoma.

Mr. Speaker, I noticed the "loud" applause of the half dozen Tories in the House this afternoon; it was because the Minister's arguments were weak.

December 17, 1987
Free Trade
The Hon. junior Minister might be able to help his own cause in Quebec if he could answer some of the questions posed today by the UPA. For instance, at its press conference this afternoon it wanted to know why nobody in the Department of Trade has been able to clarify the reason that Article 710, which mentions that Section 11 of the GATT agreement provides for import control lists, has been made subject to Article 703 in the agreement, which provides that barriers to trade between Canada and the United States will be reduced in whatever way possible, whether it be by the removal of tariffs or by the removal of quotas.
Also in its press conference this afternoon the UPA wanted to know why ice-cream, yogurt, and liquid milk were not on the import control list as was demanded by Mr. Page, the Minister of Agriculture in Quebec, and as was promised by the Minister when he spoke to the UPA a couple of weeks ago.
I will not get into the details of that speaking engagement, because it was incredibly embarrassing for the Hon. Minister.
Another concern of the UPA is why there are increased quotas for poultry and meat, an increase of some 31 million kilos to some 37 million kilos of meat per year, and an increase of 6 million dozen eggs.
At the conclusion of the press conference, the President of the UPA said that the free trade agreement raises many legal and technical problems and puts a number of problems before Quebec agricultural producers.
Could the Hon. Minister clarify these points, especially for dairy and poultry producers in the Province of Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to give the answer of a junior Minister to a senior back-bencher.
Everyone knows that we can include yogurt and ice-cream in the agreement. It is an internal question about addressing the national market. It is not really a question about free trade. Two or three weeks ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said that we had asked the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) to try to put yogurt and ice-cream on the import quota list. We are working on it now. We have said that we will check all the details of that question to find out if it is appropriate to do it. We are working on it now.
Anyway, it will not be necessary a year and a half beforehand because yogurt and ice-cream imports have decreased from 250,000 kilos to 50,000 kilos over the last two or three years.

In fact, to be more specific, in the last two or three years these imports declined to one-fifth of what they were previously. We are working on this right now. We have had several meetings about supply management with national representatives, including the Canadian Dairy Farmers and provincial organizations, especially in Quebec. These people did not take the slightly hysterical attitude we saw among some leaders in Quebec. Their approach was far more pragmatic, in that
they asked for specific questions to be dealt with. There was the issue of imitations. This comes under provincial jurisdiction. We discussed this with our provincial counterparts, including the Quebec Minister of Agriculture.
You mentioned an increase in chicken quotas. There is no increase. We have maintained import quotas at the same level, which is the average level for the past five years. Total imports for last year were lower than in 1984. Furthermore, and the Hon. Member forgot to mention this, production in the poultry sector increased 8 per cent last year in Canada. It is expected to increase by 4 per cent next year. Is there any other economic sector, any other farm sector in Canada that can say it increased production by about 13 per cent over two years, Mr. Speaker? This particular sector is in very good shape. We have no problems here. There is a production increase.
I am sure that those people ... a few minutes ago, I saw a press release issued by the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, which said they were glad to see GATT Section 11 had been recognized in the final agreement. They raised a number of other problems we will look into. I received this only a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker. This was a press conference held in Montreal, to which I was not invited, and I intend to continue our dialogue with agricultural groups in Canada, wherever they happen to be. I am sure that as soon as the Opposition Parties and the people who for philosophical reasons are opposed to free trade have changed their tune and told the Canadian people and farm producers exactly what the situation is, people will understand it is in their interests to support this Agreement and see it ratified.

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind my hon. friend that the newspapers today as a result of extensive polling, tell us that six out of 10 Canadians are against the free trade deal which the Mulroney Government has signed with the United States.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) is on record as opposing the free trade deal with the United States because of loss of Canadian sovereignty, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is on record as opposing a free trade deal, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is on the record as opposing the free trade deal, and the former Secretary of State is on record as opposing the deal. Every single candidate for the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party is on record as opposing this free trade deal with the United States because of what it will do to Canada. There was one exception, Peter Pocklington. He was the only one in favour of free trade.
The Prime Minister himself and the leading Cabinet Ministers of Canada are on the record as opposing free trade prior to the election. They then were given a mandate by the people of Canada, but the issue of free trade was never raised during the entire eight week federal election campaign. The
December 17, 1987

Prime Minister is now going to sign the agreement into effect on January 2 without any mandate from the people of Canada. The Premiers themselves who are supporting the deal have no mandate from their electorate because they never campaigned on the issue of free trade. What right does the Government of Canada have to lock Canadians into a free trade deal with the United States that will have profound implications for generations to come-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Positive implications.

-without having any mandate from the people of Canada? Could he explain why it is that the Government is signing this deal before the people of Canada have had a chance to look at the final agreement? We have had it for only three or four days, and I would guess that 99.99 per cent of Canadians have not seen the agreement, let alone studied it. Does he think this is the way a Government should do business in a democratic society?

Mr. Speaker, I think the mandate we got was to give Canadians economic prosperity. That was the mandate we received, and clearly this is what we have been delivering over these last three years. A government that can pride itself on creating more than a million jobs over the same period of time has no lessons in economy to learn from an Opposition that fought against the Auto Pact some 20 years ago and that is now fighting like a tiger because those people fear that the system we put in place during the 1960's might under a freer trade system be extended to the Canadian economy as a whole. I think we have no lessons to learn from that side, Mr. Speaker.
And if they feel like being honest, they will admit that the protectionist moves we have been facing up to very recently were not there in 1983 and 1984. Those moves came over the years, they came with the really stupendous increase in the American trade deficit, which was still at $17 billion last month. Clearly the Americans had a gut reaction when they found themselves being swamped with goods coming in from all over the world-the European Economic Community, Japan, Asia, Canada. They had a protectionist reaction. And as I explained earlier-whether the Ottawa Member listened to my speech or not-that reaction indeed was what came after 1984, the protectionist one. We had to react. Should we have adopted a wait and see attitude, and must we now have an election every three months, whenever a problem arises? We reacted, Mr. Speaker, the way a government should. We created jobs. We developed a regional development policy that is the pride of all Canadians, and when the time comes, Mr. Speaker, Canadians will pass judgement on us in the polls. I have no fear of that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin, I understand that we are expecting a messenger from the Senate, which means that my speech will probably be
Free Trade
interrupted, as it has been before in this House, by this ridiculous procedure that should have been abolished a long time ago, something which the McGrath commission recommended. Because the Government has not chosen to implement that particular recommendation of the McGrath report, I suppose we will have to suffer this absurdity at least one more time.
I am very happy to speak this afternoon. I hope that this agreement will not go through. We know that if there is an election between now and the time it is to be implemented, it will not be because we know the Government will be defeated. If, however, by some tragic turn of events it is implemented, I am glad that I will be counted for historical purposes as one of those who stood up to defend my country. I hope my grandchildren or my great-grandchildren, whoever has the misfortune of having to read through Hansard on the great free trade debate, will be able to say that their ancestors were on the side of Canada. When they are groping through the congressional library in Washington looking for records of the free trade debate that took place in that country called Canada back in 1987 they will see it there too.
I listened to the argument made by the Minister of State for Agriculture (Mr. Blais). Instead of answering the question about process he said that this agreement will bring great prosperity to Canada. Even if that were true, and I do not believe it is true, the end does not justify the means. I thought that there might be some recognition of that ethical principle by Conservative Members, but apparently, in order to foist this agreement upon the country, they have cast away any ethical norms they ever held on parliamentary process and democratic principle. The end justifies the means, and so we are to be put in the ridiculous position of debating an agreement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) proposes to sign on January 2 although the Parliament of Canada has only had an opportunity to look at the official text of it for a couple of weeks and the people of Canada themselves will not have had any opportunity to study it.
One of the enduring dishonesties of this debate has been the contention of the Government that this is just a commercial arrangement, an economic matter, nothing we should take too seriously. Canadians are asked to believe that this agreement is an ordinary agreement, that countries are in the habit of doing this sort of thing, and that opposition Members really ought not to make such a big deal of it.
Chapter One of the text of the agreement itself, the chapter entitled Objectives and Scope, says:
The objectives make clear the extent to which the Canada-United States Trade Agreement moves beyond other free-trade agreements negotiated under the GATT.
The next paragraph says:
The new Canada-United States Agreement is broader in scope as it provides for liberalization in all sectors of the economy, including agriculture. No other trade agreement includes binding commitments on trade in services, business

December 17, 1987
Free Trade
travel or investment. No other agreement provides a basis for developing new
rules-
And it goes on and on. The point is that this agreement is quite different from any other free trade agreement, but the Government wants us to believe that we are doing something quite ordinary here.
In fact, we are doing something with the united states that no other country has ever done before, no other country, regardless of its political make-up, has ever had so little selfrespect that it would even contemplate entering into an agreement like this with its neighbour or with any other country for that matter, when the minister for international trade (Miss Carney) tries to pass this agreement off as just another commercial arrangement, she is engaging in one of the most fundamentally misleading descriptions of what the government is asking Canadians to do that i can imagine.
The funny thing about this free trade agreement is that it is both more than free trade and less than free trade, where it is free trade, it is either about the kind of free trade that we have had all along, or it is about the kind of free trade that we would have achieved anyway through the continuing liberalization of trade or reduction of tariffs, on all three counts, it must be described quite differently from how the government describes it.
Why is the agreement less than free trade? We do not get the secure access to American markets that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said was the bottom line of the negotiations entered into with the United States. We will still be subject to American trade law, countervail and anti-dumping. Our exporters will still have to go through all the hassles involved in being charged under American law.
Yes, there will be a binational panel, but after the panel, there will be an appeal to a panel of judges, and if the panel of judges decides that the circumstances warrant it, it is referred back to a new binational panel. Throughout, the guidelines as to fairness will be American trade law, the very law the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade said they wanted to get out from under all along.
However, in my judgment, the more serious problem is where this agreement is about more than free trade. It includes concessions in the energy sector, the investment sector and the financial sector that cumulatively amount to a giving up of Canadian control over our own economy. The Parliamentary Secretary is making funny noises. That is not unusual. The fact is that we are giving up control over our energy, investment and financial services policies to the market-place.
Conservative Members say that that is a good thing. That fact is not lost on me. I do not think they are doing this unconsciously, although sometimes they look unconscious. They are doing this quite consciously, and that is what makes it even more reprehensible. They are quite consciously trying to lock their view of how the Canadian economy should run-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: And you are not?

-into this free trade agreement. The Parliamentary Secretary asks if I am not. No, I am not. If I were in government or elsewhere, I would not propose to enshrine the NDP view of Canada in a way that would it beyond the reach of democracy and beyond the reach of other Parliaments. We will save that for the Soviet Union or for the Conservative Government, which has so little respect for democracy and pluralism that it wants to entrench its ideas in a free trade agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: What are you worried about? You can get out of it in six months.

The Parliamentary Secretary says that we can get out of it in six months. I hope we will never even get into it. The Parliamentary Secretary knows that if by some tragic circumstance we do get into it, it will not be all that easy to get out of it. Things will have happened and we will be in a very difficult position if a future Government wanted to get out of this agreement. We hope that we can get out of it in 1988 through the election of a new Government that will not have anything to do with this agreement. For that matter, 1989 will do, any time within the constitutional limitation of this Government. In either 1988 or 1989, we will tear up the agreement, but tear it up we will. Should the worst possible thing happen and, by some quirk of ugly fate, this gang of bandits over here were re-elected, that is what I mean when I talk about the difficulty of getting out of the agreement in the future.
I said that the agreement is about less than free trade and more than free trade. Where it is about free trade, it is about the kind of thing that would have happened anyway the kind of thing we did not have to give up our sovereignty to get. Tariffs have been going down since 1945, and 80 per cent of our trade with the United States is tariff-free now. What is left would probably have been reduced over time in any event.
What was the big deal? The big deal was that these people over here were spooked, were made scared and by the protectionist mood in the U.S. Congress. Instead of trying to find long-term solutions and counteract U.S. protectionism in other ways, the Government, "Said we cannot do it. If we cannot beat them, let us join them". It did not even try to beat them. It gave up on the global process. It gave up on the multilateral process. It said, "Let us get in under those American skirts and hope we will be looked after. Let us see if we can get a sweetheart arrangement". That is what the Government did, and Members opposite have the nerve to get up and talk about confidence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You are not telling the truth again.

They have absolutely no confidence in Canada. The only confidence the Tories have in Canada is the confidence that somehow we can become as much like the Americans as we have to in order to be competitive. That is not a
December 17, 1987

surprise. What we have among the Tory back-benchers is a lot of neo-Americans anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: A lot of what?
Neo-Americans. Almost as bad as neoConservatives. People who spent their childhood singing for the American company president when he came to town every once in a while to check on his empire.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Neo-communist and the NDP, same thing.
Whatever happened to the Tory view of Canada? Sir John A. Macdonald and John George Diefen-baker must be spinning in their graves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Listen to who the socialists are quoting!
1 do not mind quoting real Tories because from time to time they were on to something about the nature of this country, especially historically.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: The best thing that happened to us was when you left the Tory Party.

John Diefenbaker had a northern vision of Canada. What have we got over there? Dallas! A southern vision of Canada, a Canada more like Alabama than the Canada we have come to know and which most Canadians, except for Tories, have come to value.
If you check the record, all the things jeopardized by this agreement are things the Conservatives never liked in the first place. Social programs. Who have New Democrats had to fight over the years to put in place the social programs threatened by this agreement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: People do not believe that, Bill.

Conservatives. Who have New Democrats had to fight over the years to get controls on foreign investment? Conservatives. Who have New Democrats had to fight in order to have a sane policy energy and not just sell off everything as fast as we can? Conservatives. It is no coincidence that when we look at what this agreement puts in jeopardy, it is being put in place by a Conservative Government.
I also have a word to say about what this agreement means in light of some of the things that have been said in the last few weeks about the federal Government's alleged ability to impose this agreement without provincial consent, or about cooperative federalism. I remember the Tories in 1981 and 1982. Oh, how they sung the praises of co-operative federalism. Oh, how they vilified any Government that would consider changing the Constitution of Canada without substantial, or even at that time unanimous, provincial consent. Yet what do they propose to do now? By President Reagan's own admission, they propose to change the economic constitution of this country. The Government proposes to change the economic constitution of Canada without seeking a mandate, without a consensus, and without the kind of unanimity we voted for not
Free Trade
too long ago on constitutional matters when we voted for the Meech Lake Accord.
Oh, was that not a day for federal-provincial reconciliation? Nothing would be done without unanimity. The rhetoric flowed about what a wonderful achievement that was for federalism and co-operation and harmony. Frankly, I feel as though I have been had. I tried as best I could to believe all that stuff when I voted for the Meech Lake Accord. I feel as though I have been had by the Prime Minister when he gets up and talks about what he will do and to hell with the provinces.
I feel as though I have been had by the Premier of Quebec, too, because I got up and voted for Quebec's right to a distinct society. I thought that was a great victory for Quebec and Canada. Frankly, I feel stabbed in the back by the Premier of Quebec who has now said to the rest of Canada, through his support for this free trade agreement, that our distinct non-Quebec Canadian society is not worth fighting for as far as he is concerned. That can be sacrificed to his convictions about the alleged economic benefits of this agreement.
I feel double-crossed with respect to the question of a distinct society. As a non-Quebec Canadian I feel that Canada as a whole is entitled to economic structures and relationships which enable us to preserve and enhance our distinct society. I hope the Premier of Quebec will reconsider his support for this agreement on that basis.
Now we come to the question of whether the Government has a mandate for this agreement. By now Canadians who are listening and Members of Parliament have heard time and time again about how the Conservatives ran in 1984 on the basis that they would not enter into a free trade agreement.
We ran on jobs.
The Hon. Member says they ran on jobs. Who did not run on jobs? Give me a break. We all ran on jobs and what we argue about is what will create jobs-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: And what has created jobs.

-and what jobs will be created and all that sort of thing. To run on jobs is not a mandate to enter into this kind of agreement. In fact, the free trade agreement the Prime Minister wants to sign on January 2 is much more threatening than the kind of free trade that he rejected when he said the issue had been settled in 1911. The free trade that was debated in 1911 was a question of tariffs. It was actually a trade agreement because it had only to do with tariffs.
If the Prime Minister thought in 1983 that the kind of trade agreement contemplated in 1911 threatened Canadian sovereignty, why in heaven's name would he propose to sign an agreement on January 2 that goes way beyond the concept he found so threatening in 1983? Why? You want to know what I think? It is because this kind of agreement with Canada was on the American agenda. This is something the Americans wanted Canada to enter into. It is no coincidence that before

December 17, 1987
Free Trade
American Ambassador Robinson left Canada he set this in motion. It just so happened that along came Brian, the perfect sucker for this kind of an agreement. Since Confederation Canada has become a significantly just and peaceful country. In a very short time, historically speaking, it is to be bargained away in the interests of entrenching neo-Conservative view of Canada.
It would be a tragedy beyond all proportion if this should ever pass. However, 1 have enough confidence in Canadians to know that, if given the chance in a general election, they will tell the Prime Minister that they want to keep Canada and trade him.

Mr. Speaker, with the committee 1 had an opportunity to travel in western Canada with the Hon. Member from Winnipeg. We heard from groups such as the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency. Representatives of that organization expressed concern about increased quotas for eggs and poultry while not getting new access to American markets because of the differences between our systems. We have a supply management system with government controls, although that system will be sorely tested. Article 701.3 of the agreement reads:
Neither Party, including any public entity that it establishes or maintains, shall sell agricultural goods for export to the territory of the other Party at a price below the acquisition price of the goods plus any storage, handling or other costs incurred by it with respect to those goods.
That causes an incredible problem for supply management agencies such as CEMA which produces eggs on an administered price basis. When there are surpluses, they break the eggs and use them as processed egg products. Some of that is disposed of in the United States because there is not an adequate market for it here. That may seem like a relatively small item in the over-all context of an agency the size of CEMA, and perhaps it is, but it points out the danger of proceeding hell-bent for leather on this agreement. The committee reported last Thursday night and the final text came out on Friday. We are debating it for three short days this week and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will sign the deal on January 2.
According to the legal advice which this agency has received, they will have to sell this agricultural commodity at the same price for which they bought it in Canada plus handling costs, even though it is a surplus commodity which cannot possibly be disposed of at that price. That is the danger of such a rushed agreement which contains unworkable clauses.
I do not know what will happen to this agency. This issue may have to be negotiated if the agreement is ever implemented. However, it is certainly not a workable agreement. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary or someone else will be able to respond to the concerns of agricultural groups like CEMA.

Mr. Speaker, the point of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) is well made. He mentioned that we spent time together travelling with the committee listening to a balanced representation of Canadians making submissions on the free trade agreement.
Although over-all the committee was a farce, given that we did not have the agreement and were only able to report after the final negotiations were complete, certain witnesses who were supporters of the agreement were more honest about the agreement than the Government has ever been. We were, therefore, able to learn various things about the agreement from its supporters.
With respect to marketing boards, we learned from the Grocery Products Manufacturing Association-hardly a cell of the socialist conspiracy-that marketing boards would be at risk under this agreement. A lowering of tariffs and the continued existence of our supply management system as it is now constituted would be incompatible. We have been saying that all along, but when we said it it was NDP fear-mongering. Now the Grocery Products Manufacturing Association has said that.
We have said for some time that this agreement would infringe on the right of provinces to control energy prices. Every time we tried to get the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) to say that in the House, we failed. She would say that it was another NDP tactic. Former Premier Peter Lougheed of Alberta came before the committee and said that that is what the agreement means. I suppose he is part of the socialist conspiracy too, distorting the meaning of this agreement. He said that the provinces would no longer have the power to set a domestic price for, in Alberta's case, natural gas and oil. That was okay with him. It is not okay with me, but at least he was honest about the agreement.
We have said that this agreement will eventually mean the end of the Crow benefit and the current economic structure of western Canada, and we were dismissed. However, the Western Wheat Growers came before us-again hardly an arm of the NDP-and said that over time this will mean the end of the Crow benefit, which may have to be replaced with payments to producers, which is something a lot of Tories are in favour of anyway. At least the Western Wheat Growers were honest with the committee, in a way the Government has not been, about the effect of this agreement.
We have said that our social programs are put in jeopardy by this agreement because they be taken into account when judging which country may have a competitive advantage over the other. They said we were being hysterical when we said that. However, representatives of the business community in Vancouver and National Sea in Halifax came before us and said that some companies invest in Canada because our social programs are a competitive advantage for them.
That may be good, but in the next five to seven years when we are negotiating what it means to have a level playing field,
December 17, 1987

social programs will be included in calculations for competitive advantage.
It could come through Canadians arguing that the tax burden they must bear in order to continue to fund our programs makes them uncompetitive, or the Americans could argue that our programs are an unfair advantage to companies which locate here in Canada. In either case, the unassailable point that I believe we are making is that social programs will become part and parcel of the negotiations when we talk about competitive advantage. That was admitted by people who supported the agreement.
Although the over-all committee process was a farce, it had bright moments. Those bright moments were not only when opponents of the agreement came before the committee and articulated why this agreement is a sell-out of Canada and its future, but when supporters of the agreement appeared before the committee and were more forthcoming about the true consequences of this agreement than the Government has ever had the parliamentary or moral decency to be with us or with the Canadian people.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I think we must emphasize over and over again that in this debate we are not discussing theoretical free trade. We are not discussing the pros and cons of textbook free trade, we are debating and discussing a very specific trade agreement between the United States and Canada which was concluded on October 4, 1987. It is that deal we are examining.
I say this because in listening to the discussion across the country and in this House one gets the impression that individuals are debating free trade as they learned it at university.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak first in the adjournment debate this evening. I was expecting to speak second.
I want to tell you a story, Mr. Speaker, about a friend of mine. This particular friend is a black Canadian woman. I have known her for a number of years. She was born in Canada, and understandably she becomes very upset when people ask her where she comes from. This friend of mine is a widow, but she was married to a black Canadian who was also born in this country. They have two children. My friend tells me this story that I wish to share with you tonight, Mr. Speaker, of the day when one of her daughters came home from school. Both of her daughters attend schools in my constituency. One day one of her daughters came home from school and told her mother that she was going to paint herself white. She said that because of the remarks that had been made to her by her friends and her schoolmates, remarks that obviously caused her a great deal of upset and concern. That story had a deep impact on me.
There is no way that myself, you, Mr. Speaker, and the Parliamentary Secretary, for that matter, could possibly understand the things that went through the mind of that young black Canadian girl, her father, and her mother on that particular occasion. To me it was a very touching story.
It made me think back to the days when I joined the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada in 1956. I did it because I believed at that time, and I truly believe today, that the Progressive Conservative Party stands for equality; equality of opportunity and equality of the person regardless of race, colour, or creed. That is what the Progressive Conservative Party is all about to me, and that is what Canada is all about to me. It is because of that I have been so happy and pleased that the current Government, the Government that I was elected to support and do support, was the very first Government in this country to introduce employment equity legislation for women, native people, the disabled, and visible minorities.
I was also pleased when the Government, for the very first time ever in this country, introduced an affirmative action program in the Public Service of Canada for visible minorities. I was especially pleased to hear the Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) earlier this fall stand up in the House and indicate in answer to one of my questions that the Government and the Treasury Board had instituted targets for
visible minorities in the Public Service, targets that had never been in place before.
Against this background, Mr. Speaker, you can imagine how disappointed I was to start receiving calls from people in the Public Service indicating that the affirmative action program put in place was not working. I might not have been particularly concerned if it had come from only one or two sources, but I have had those concerns raised to me by people who work in the Department of Justice, people who work in the Department of Supply and Services, people who work in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, people who work in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, people who work in Treasury Board itself, people who work in the Department of Employment and Immigration, people who work in the Department of Labour, people who work in the Department of the Environment, and people who work for the Public Service Commission of Canada, which is supposed to be there to make sure that everybody receives equal treatment.
These people tell me that the programs which have been put in place are not working. In fact, they say that instead of actually increasing the number of visible minorities in the Public Service, they are actually decreasing because of retirements and lay-offs. They say that instead of getting promotions they are standing still. After years of the former Liberal Government doing nothing about seeing that visible minorities in the Public Service were promoted to management and senior management positions, they had hoped that with this Government there would be a change. However, they are not seeing that change, and those are the concerns which they are conveying to me.
This is why I want to raise this question with the Parliamentary Secretary tonight. I want him to consider it and answer it very carefully.
Personally, I want to be part of a Government which is colour blind, part of a Government which promotes people on merit, part of a Government where everyone is considered equal, and part of a Government where people do not have to think about going home and painting themselves white in order to be treated fairly.
With that in mind, I ask the Parliamentary Secretary what the Government will do about it. Will it follow through with an effective affirmative action program, one which has specific targets, not only globally for the whole Public Service but department by department and position by position? What will the Government do about it? I want to hear from him that he will ensure that the program is put into effect and that he is prepared to put his own position as a Parliamentary Secretary, and that of the Minister's, on the line if that does not occur.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for raising this very important issue. I recall that Mr. Diefenbaker used to speak about hyphenated
December 17, 1987

Canadians and how insulted he was at the concept of having to be registered as a hyphenated Canadian. I recall in 1945 when I had to register under the National Selective Service Act that I could not register as a Canadian in those days. I had to register as a German Mennonite. I am glad that those days have passed, yet it requires continual vigilance to ensure that all of us see each other as Canadians and not as foreign nationals.
I assure the Hon. Member that the Government is committed to addressing the employment concerns of visible minorities and has taken many positive steps to entrench employment equity principles and practices in the federal Public Service.
In 1985 visible minorities were designated as an employment equity target group, and a 14-member advisory committee to the President of the Treasury Board on the employment of visible minorities was established.
Since then the following initiatives have been undertaken: preparation of a report on the availability of qualified members of visible minority groups; creation of special training modules for Public Service managers on visible minorities and employment equity; design of a special orientation module for newly recruited visible minorities in the Public Service; revision of the application for employment form so that visible minorities can self-identify; initiation of a survey to obtain current figures on the numbers of public servants in each target group; and establishment of an automated system to track visible minority employees through the recruitment and staffing process.
In June, 1986 a special program was designed specifically to meet the needs of visible minorities. This program consists of $10.5 million and 300 person-years to be allocated over a three-year period between 1986 and 1989, an office of services for visible minority groups within the Public Service Commission to provide over-all program co-ordination and evaluation, and a network of regional visible minority co-ordinators across Canada.
As recently as August, 1987 we further demonstrated our commitment to this group by approving the establishment of numerical targets for visible minority groups, and I am sure that the Hon. Member is looking for that. This decision was made in response to the recommendations of the president's advisory committee, which is sensitive to the concerns of target group members. The numerical targets will be established by Departments for a three year period beginning April 1, 1988. Now visible minority groups are on an equal footing with the other target groups in the Public Service, women, disabled persons and aboriginal peoples, who have had numerical objectives since 1985-86.
To set these targets, Departments are being asked to compare the number of visible minority employees to the availability of members of these groups in the Canadian labour force. According to the 1981 census data, this figure is slightly
Adjournment Debate
more than 4 per cent. The visible minority population of the Public Service was identified as 1.7 per cent by a 1985 survey, which is the latest data available.
I am pleased to say that our Government is responding positively by addressing the employment concerns of visible minorities. We are determined to eliminate inequities in the workplace so that all Canadians are able to obtain their fair share of employment opportunities in the Public Service.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-RIGHTS OF EARLY RETIREES- REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-RIGHTS OF EARLY RETIREES- REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back to a an issue of utmost importance for Members of this House and the general public. This is the time of the year when we wish one another a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. It reminds me that in December of 1985, the Government chose to make a very special gift to older workers who were on UI benefits and where looking for a job.
On January 5, 1986, everybody suddenly realized that from then on, people who had lost their job and were entitled to benefits of an employer-sponsored pension plan would have their UI benefits reduced by the same amount. After 17 months of struggle by older workers, people from the Quebec City area, the Montreal area and from all parts of Canada, we succeeded. The Government backed down and 46,000 persons were reimbursed the equivalent of $10,000. Unfortunately, other people also took an early retirement or lost their job on December 31. Just imagine. It is December 31 and 1000 people at Quebec Hydro . . . There are 2000 people in this same predicament in Canada. The workers finished working on December 31 and that was it, the plant was closed. They are entitled to their severance pay and their unused sick leave. On January 1, the employment centers are closed. So, these people went to manpower centres on January 4 to ask for their unemployment insurance benefits. They were told by officials: You must first use up your benefits for your two weeks vacation and sick leave and then come back. These people went back at the end of that period, following the advice given by Members of Parliament, by the Minister of Employment and Immigration, by officials at the Department of Employment; these people went back to ask for their benefits on the date when they were to become eligible, around January 15. However, they suddenly discovered that the legislation . . . there are 2,000 people in Canada who find themselves in that situation today, they had to go in early retirement before January 5, 1986, as the Government requested, in order to be reimbursed, but because they made that request after, the request was rejected and the person is penalized. So, I submit that this measure is unfair. It is a fact that in the Laurentian region, for instance, when people appealed this decision, their appeal was upheld and they are getting a refund from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In the Montreal region, on the other hand, the decision was maintained. In the Quebec region, it was the other way around.

December 17, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be important to see some justice here. I think it would be appropriate, just before the holiday season, for the Government to examine its conscience and pay for its sins with a little generosity. It should give refunds to those 2,000 people.
There is another side as well. An unfortunate one, and I hope the Government and the Minister of State (Senior Citizens) (Mr. Hees) will manage to rectify this. I am referring to the fact that from now on, every person, every older worker-and that is discrimination-who loses his job and has to withdraw his pension benefits-a number of businesses in Montreal are closing, including Coleco-while that person is looking for a new job, and after withdrawing the pension benefits he paid for, the contributions he is now entitled to put in his pocket, including the employer's contribution for which he opted in lieu of a pay increase-now these people can kiss their unemployment insurance cheque goodbye.
On the other hand, if that same person withdrew the same amount, say $500, from a registered retirement savings plan, he would be entitled to the full amount of his cheque. We cannot tolerate the Government maintaining this kind of discrimination and injustice in its treatment of older workers.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the Parliamentary Secretary would provide more details on what the Government has decided to do.
First of all, will the Minister, since it is the season to be generous, say: Okay, we have 2,000 people in this gray area, and now all those who have a job termination certificate, who left their jobs but were looking for a new job before January 5, 1986, will receive a refund because it wasn't their fault they couldn't come and apply for unemployment insurance benefits? Those 2,000 people should get an immediate refund of the money the Government owes them.
Subsequently, in the next Speech from the Throne or the next Budget or by issuing instructions the way they did in 1985 when Cabinet decided to pick on older workers, perhaps he could change the system and rectify his mistake by removing any hint of discrimination and letting anyone, whatever their source of income-the way it was before-be entitled to the full amount of his unemployment insurance benefits, provided he can prove he is still looking for work.
When a young person is out of work, he goes to the unemployment insurance office, and they don't ask him: Do you have other income? If he is forty or fifty years old, they don't ask: Do you have rental income? Do you have investment income? Are you getting any income from an RRSP? They say: You have paid so many weeks worth of unemployment insurance benefits so you are eligible for that number of weeks. Here is the money. As soon as you start working again, as soon as you start receiving employment-related earnings, let us know and we will stop your benefits, and so forth.
Today, however, only a person who has a registered employee/employer pension plan has his unemployment insurance payments reduced or completely cut off.
I hope that in this holiday season, at a time when we should be generous to these older workers, the Parliamentary Secretary will stop to consider that these are people who worked for twenty, thirty or forty years by the sweat of their brow and were able to save a little money. We have to remember that these people paid every penny of their unemployment insurance contributions. They were never on unemployment insurance, and now if the plant closes down, they lose their jobs, and they file for unemployment insurance while they are looking for a job, they are penalized. That is injustice, pure and simple.
So in this holiday season, I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will say the Government is going to give a refund to those
2,000	people and that he will make the requisite changes for the coming year to amend the unemployment insurance system.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-RIGHTS OF EARLY RETIREES- REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the Hon. Member that the issues of unemployment and unemployment insurance are very important and in no way would we minimize them. I hope he would agree with me, though, that the best gift we have given to the people of Montreal and Quebec is the creation in the last three years of over a million jobs. Jobs are ever so much better than unemployment or unemployment insurance. I think the thousands of people in Montreal who are now working as a result of the policies of this Government will recognize that.
I would like to answer the Hon. Member's question of March 20. He will recall that Bill C-50 became effective on April 5, 1987. While maintaining the principle that persons who have retired should not use UI as supplementary income, Bill C-50 ensured that workers who take other employment after their retirement and then work long enough to re-qualify for UI benefits will receive those benefits without any deduction of the previous pension income.
The Bill permitted the retroactive re qualification back to January 5, 1986. As well, the Government amended the pension regulations to permit re-qualification as of April 5, 1987. These changes to the pension legislation are consistent with the Government's belief that persons who have retired from the labour market should not look to unemployment insurance as a supplementary source of income.
As well, Bill C-50 draws a clear and simple line to ensure that there is fairness in the transition provisions. The rule is simply this. Those who applied for unemployment insurance prior to January 5, 1986, that is to say those who applied under the previous rules, have had their entitlement to benefits determined under the previous rules. Equally straightforward,
December 17, 1987

those who applied for benefits on or after January 5, 1986, are governed by the new rules.
In respect of the alleged discrimination between Registered Retirement Savings Plans and employment-generated pensions, it should be noted that RRSPs are a form of personal savings much like investments in long-term securities which eventually provide an annuity. Investment income derived from personal savings has long been regarded as having no relation to income arising from employment and therefore as non-earnings for unemployment insurance purposes. There is no intention of changing this position.
On the other hand, both UI and employment-generated pensions have as a general intention to compensate a person upon becoming unemployed. To avoid double indemnification it is therefore a sound principle to treat retirement pensions as earnings. Bill C-50 and related regulatory amendments provide adequate relief to older workers. For those who work long enough after the start of their pension income to establish a new claim for benefit, the pension income will cease to be regarded as earnings for UI purposes.
I hope the Hon. Member will agree that those individuals who have saved money and invested it in an RRSP should not be penalized for their foresight and planning. This Government is not embarrassed at all about the fact it rewards and encourages those people who save for the hard times that could lie ahead.

Mr. Speaker, it was on September 10, 1985, a bit over two years ago, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) gave his historic speech to this House on the subject of Arctic sovereignty, something that had been neglected for many, many years by the previous Government. At that time he announced a number of initiatives, many of which are now on the way. Those include additional sovereignty overflights in the Arctic, better defence systems, construction of a Polar 8 ice-breaker, and others.
There are two initiatives that I want to address this afternoon. One was his statement that there would be an immediate adoption of a Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act. Second, that there would immediately commence talks with the U.S. on co-operation in Arctic waters on the basis of full respect for Canadian sovereignty.
In the Minister's announcement there is no connection between the two. One was not dependent on the other. In fact, shortly after the statement, Bill C-104, the Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act, was introduced in the House. It never got very far and died on the Order Paper shortly thereafter.
Adjournment Debate
Those of who have a suspicious frame of mind might think there is some connection between the two and the Government is reluctant to introduce the Act until the talks with the U.S. have been brought to a conclusion. That is despite assurances to the contrary by government spokesmen. If that in fact is not the case, why has the Government not reintroduced that Act? That was my question to the Minister on October 6, 1987. That is not the first time I asked that question and it was not the first time I received the same answer, "Soon". That is a very popular answer with the Government.
This is an important issue at this time because there has just been released to the press-and I know not how because it was supposed to have been confidential-an initial draft of the Arctic co-operation agreement, which is taking a lot longer to negotiate than did the free trade agreement. We have had some inclinations from the press as to what it might contain. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that such an agreement will be signed in the future. What we know of it leaves a number of outstanding questions.
We still do not know whether the U.S. will recognize our claims to certain offshore areas or whether the agreement will only be an agreement to disagree, as is the present case. We know that permission will have to be granted, or at least sought, if the United States wants to send an ice-breaker through the Northwest Passage. Is this only if they want to go through the Prince of Wales Strait, which is less than 24 miles wide? If they intend to go through the M'Clure Strait, which is blocked with ice most of the time, would they still request Canadian permission?
Unanswered questions exist with respect to U.S. naval operations in the Arctic, which we understand is not to be included in this agreement. Canadians have a right to know whether there exists any agreement with the United States concerning their notification of us or request for permission from us if they want to engage in naval operations in the waters claimed by Canada.
When we ask those questions of the Government we get a rather equivocating answer. The Government will not tell us whether such an agreement exists or whether the U.S. tells the Government if they are there. Canadians really want to have these questions answered.
This afternoon I urge that the Canadian Laws OffShore Application Act be reintroduced as soon as possible and then be proceeded with through second and third readings. I would like to have the whole question completed. I look forward to the day when there will be navigation through the Northwest Passage, when it becomes a waterway open to vessels of all nations for commercial purposes, so long as they keep to the rules which Canada ought to and has every right to apply to vessels navigating in those waters.

Mr. Speaker, I want to

commend the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) for the work he has done in representing his constituency, especially on the question he has just raised, which impinges on his constituency probably more than on any other. He has shown his usual consistency in representing his constituents to Parliament and to the Government.
Following the 1985 voyage of the U.S. Coastguard icebreaker Polar Sea, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) made a statement in the House concerning Canadian sovereignty, particularly in the Arctic. Among the measures that he announced on behalf of the Government was immediate talks with the United States on co-operation in Arctic waters on the basis of full respect for Canadian sovereignty.
Since then the two sides have exchanged draft texts and progress was achieved on practical arrangements that might govern shipping activity in the Canadian Arctic archipelago and off the coast of Alaska. The matter was also raised at ministerial level on several occasions and between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan at the Washington Summit in March, 1986, and the Ottawa Summit in April, 1987.
The Prime Minister and President Reagan agreed at the Ottawa Summit to inject new impetus to the discussions already under-way and pledged their determination to find a solution based on mutual respect for sovereignty and our security and other interests.
With respect to the details of the discussion, we are seeking a practical arrangement that would require Canada's prior consent each and every time the United States wishes to send a U.S. government-owned or government-operated ice-breaker, like the Polar Sea, through the Northwest Passage.
With respect to the Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act, the Government considers that this is an important Bill and is committed to bringing it before the House shortly. I know the Member for Western Arctic will be very closely involved in the passage of that legislation.
